missions.title: The Missing Tuesday
missions.knowledgeQuestion: What does a claim become when it travels without its limits or its source?
missions.stake: If the missing Tuesday stays missing, readers walk to a closed hall, and blame the people inside.

objectives.title: Follow the passage to the City of Copies.
Compare the date on the press proof with the original trial log.
Compare who signed the press proof and who signed the landing copy.
Set out the checked copies with Printer Lark.
Read the route book and talk through the two delivery paths with Lending Keeper Mina.
Help Mina get the trial time and the source back onto the public copies.

missions.title: At Reading Distance
missions.knowledgeQuestion: Who can check a notice from the place where they wait?

objectives.title: Prepare a copy that a reader can check from the waiting bench.

missions.title: Two Lines Back
missions.knowledgeQuestion: How can a reader verify that a correction restored what was lost?

objectives.title: Check the corrected trial proof against the landing copy.

characters.name: Lending Keeper Mina
characters.role: Keeper of the public lending hall

dialogue.speaker: copies-presskeeper
dialogue.text: The landing sent back a notice I barely recognised. The words about a quicker return line are still there. The start and the signature have changed. Line up the proof here and the copy at the landing. Keep the archive line close enough to compare each time.

dialogue.speaker: copies-presskeeper
dialogue.text: We lost Tuesday at the press and the clerk’s name at the landing. The archive keeper wants to know which sheet changed first. Mina needs to know whether the wording describes a trial or sounds like a rule. The same three sheets can serve either job.

options.text: Keep the three sheets in the order the wording changed.
Pin the missing time and source beside the copies that dropped them.
Give me a moment with the copies.

dialogue.speaker: copies-presskeeper
dialogue.text: Set the dated log first, then the press proof and the stall copy. A keeper can trace each change to a sheet and see where it entered the chain. Mina can still point to Tuesday on the first sheet when someone hears the last one as an everyday rule.

dialogue.speaker: copies-presskeeper
dialogue.text: Pin the day under the line it limits and the clerk’s name under the line they observed. Mina can point to the words that turn an ordinary claim into a record of one trial. I’ll leave each strip with its edition so the keeper can still see when it dropped out.

dialogue.speaker: copies-presskeeper
dialogue.text: I’ve kept the comparison here. Find the archive route book and look for Mina at the landing. She knows which copy readers actually see.

dialogue.speaker: copies-presskeeper
dialogue.text: A printer asked me to shorten the new sheet. I cut a spare title line. The trial’s day and the clerk’s log still sit beside the claim. A printer once told me the Nexus printed a neat line and lost its limit. I’ve heard the story twice, both times from her.

dialogue.speaker: copies-lendingkeeper
dialogue.text: Someone left a book on the steps and went home. They read ‘return-slip line’ on a stall copy and thought the hall would turn them away. The archive route book tells us which copies reach the door and which travel with the runners.

dialogue.speaker: copies-lendingkeeper
dialogue.text: The hall receives full sheets at the door. The runners pin short notes at the stalls. The binders at the door read the names and dates. Market runners learn the stall marks and look to those first. Whoever copies our correction will know one route better than the other.

options.text: Mark on the route book who can read a sheet at the hall door.
Mark where the runners can attach a correction to an older copy.

dialogue.speaker: copies-lendingkeeper
dialogue.text: I’ll mark the landing stall too. A person queuing for a cart may see the stall copy before they reach the hall.

dialogue.speaker: copies-lendingkeeper
dialogue.text: The stall route carries a short correction quickly. I’ll keep the hall’s door on the route as a place to check the original.

dialogue.speaker: copies-lendingkeeper
dialogue.text: I have the route book here. Bring Lark’s comparison when you’re ready. Any copy we change needs both the trial day and the source.

dialogue.speaker: copies-lendingkeeper
dialogue.text: Lark’s proof shows how the words reached us. A keeper uses it to check who made the observation. A reader deciding whether to enter needs to know what the words cover. A full sheet is easy to check at the hall door. Strips reach both runner routes while the stalls are open. Keep the dated old copy so anyone can trace our correction.

options.text: Hang a full reprint with the trial time and source beside the claim.
Send correction strips to the existing copies with both time and source.
Hold on to the signed original for now.

dialogue.speaker: copies-lendingkeeper
dialogue.text: The full correction is up at the door. A reader who asks who recorded the shorter line can find the clerk’s log from here. The stall copies still carry the old words. The dated old sheet sits behind the reprint in the record pouch.

dialogue.speaker: copies-lendingkeeper
dialogue.text: The runners will put the day and the clerk’s name beside the old words on each stall copy. A stallholder can see why the observation applies to one trial. A keeper tracing the change can still find the original in the archive.

dialogue.speaker: copies-lendingkeeper
dialogue.text: A reader left a note at the landing. Please take a look. We should hear what a person took from the copy before we send another one.

dialogue.speaker: copies-lendingkeeper
dialogue.text: The reprint carries the day and the clerk’s name, but the reader still asked for permission. The log tells us what happened to one queue. The hall register answers who can enter. Keep the trial where a reader can check it, and give the entry rule its own line.

options.text: Give the entry rule its own line below the trial on the reprint.
I’ll return to the door first.

dialogue.speaker: copies-lendingkeeper
dialogue.text: The stall correction restores the day and the clerk’s name. One reader took that as proof of an entry rule. The log tells us what happened to one queue. The hall register answers who can enter. Give the runners a separate line that can travel with each correction.

options.text: Ask the runners to put a separate entry line beside each correction.
I’ll return to the landing first.

dialogue.speaker: copies-lendingkeeper
dialogue.text: The reader has picked up their book from the steps. They can see Tuesday’s quicker return line and the entry rule together. A cartographer at Seagrass Steps has sent a chart with a similar missing edge. The Nexus passage is open.

dialogue.speaker: copies-lendingkeeper
dialogue.text: One runner is already back. A stallkeeper reads the entry line aloud beside the trial. The runner has brought an open question from Seagrass Steps about the edge of a chart. The Nexus passage is open.

dialogue.speaker: copies-lendingkeeper
dialogue.text: A reader told me the note is still small from the place where they wait. I can use the old place for the two narrow titles, or we can print one larger copy for that bench.

options.text: Put a larger copy by the bench with separate lines for the trial and entry rule.

dialogue.speaker: copies-lendingkeeper
dialogue.text: There’s room for both lines here. I’ll put the log name in the same type as the date. A reader can check the trial without carrying the whole sheet over to the door.

hints.text: There’s a new crossing from the Nexus.
A printer wants to know why the same record says different things in different places.
Return to the Nexus after adding the Metalworks cart record.
Take the passage to the City of Copies. It leads to the source archive.
Lark’s first proof is on the table in the Print Workshop.
Compare what still appears in the same words on both sheets.
Line up both margins and check which one lost the day of the trial.
At the first press proof, choose Line up the time marks and Line up the source lines. Check where Tuesday disappeared.
Find the runners’ copy on the Lending Hall Landing.
Follow the clerk’s name from the press proof to the posted notice.
Use the comparison table to check the source as well as the time.
At the runner’s landing copy, choose Line up the time marks and Line up the source lines. Check which sheet still has a named source.
The original gives a time and names who recorded it.
Check how time and attribution travel on their own lines.
Use the press proof and the landing copy. Line up the time and source lines at both.
After comparing both editions, speak with Lark and choose how to preserve the trail of changes.
A sheet and a strip reach different readers.
Find the route book in the archive. It records where printed messages travel.
Take the route book’s paths to Mina at the landing.
Ask Mina who waits by the door or looks at the stalls, and decide how to mark those two routes.
Restore the words beside the claim that needs them.
A new sheet reaches the door. A correction strip can reach stalls that still use the old copies.
Talk to Mina when the two editions and the distribution route have been checked.
Choose a full reprint for the hall or send correction strips to existing copies. Save an older version for the record either way.
A reader has found the correction but still has a question.
Check the note by the landing.
Read the reader’s message about bringing a slip into the hall.
Keep the reader’s question with the exact claim the clerk’s trial log supported. The two ask about different things.
The clerk’s log describes a line on one trial day. The reader is asking who can enter.
Leave space for both facts. Neither replaces the other.
Talk to Mina after reading the reader’s message.
Revise the reprint or the correction strip to explain that the slip was for returns. The entrance remains open.
The landing’s small type is hard to read from the bench.
Keep the date and the person who wrote the log where a reader can see both.
Talk with Mina after revising the public record.
Ask for a larger copy with the trial and the entry rule on separate lines.
The repair can be checked against the copy that reached the landing.
Look for the corrected trial proof near the runner’s copy.
Align its time marks and source lines as you did at the press.
Tuesday’s trial and the Lending Clerk’s log should both reappear. The access rule has its own notice.

journal.title: The missing Tuesday
journal.text: The press copy lost the trial day. The landing copy lost the source. I restored both, then helped Mina keep the trial result and the hall’s entry rule on separate lines.

journal.title: At reading distance
journal.text: We put a larger copy beside the bench. The trial day and the clerk’s log stayed together. The entry rule had a line of its own.

moments.did: You followed a reader’s different interpretation and revised the public notice.
You kept the full record in reach of a reader at the waiting bench.
